\chapter{Breakfast, Fruit And Something Sweet}
\label{ch:el-desayuno-y-la-fruta}
\hlchaptermodality{367}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say el desayuno, la fruta, la naranja, la patata and el azúcar, and name the first meal of the day and what goes into it.}

Complete ES-C367-azucar: name the first meal of the day and four things that can go into it.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el desayuno]{el desayuno — the meal that undoes a fast}

\label{lesson:ES-C367-desayuno}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the stairs}, then \emph{the wardrobe}. (\emph{La escalera}; \emph{el armario}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el pan — what is most often on the plate at this hour.
  \item el café — the drink beside it.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{de-sa-YU-no}, four beats with the weight on the third. The \emph{y} here is a consonant, close to the \emph{y} of English \emph{yes}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el desayuno} — \textquotedblleft{}breakfast.\textquotedblright{}

Take the word in two pieces. \textbf{Ayuno} is a fast — going without food. \textbf{Des-} undoes whatever follows it. So \emph{desayuno} is the \textbf{un-fasting}: the meal that cancels a night of not eating.

English builds its own word out of exactly that idea, out of Germanic parts rather than Latin ones: \textbf{break} plus \textbf{fast}. Two languages, two vocabularies, one thought.

Then English does it a second time, by borrowing instead of building. \textbf{Dinner} came from Old French \emph{disner}, and behind \emph{disner} stands a late Latin verb meaning to break a fast. \emph{Breakfast} and \emph{dinner} are the same sentence in one language, one half of it homegrown and the other imported — which is how the imported half drifted all the way to the evening without anybody noticing what it said.

The Latin family behind \emph{ayuno} left two more marks on English:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{jejune} — thin, meagre, unsatisfying. A jejune argument leaves you hungry.
  \item \textbf{the jejunum} — a stretch of the small intestine. Early anatomists opened bodies and kept finding that particular stretch empty, so they called it \textquotedblleft{}the fasting one.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

One Latin root for going without: a meal that ends it, a criticism that means it, and a piece of your own body that got the name by accident of dissection.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now name the first meal of the day: \emph{el desayuno}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el desayuno}
  \item \emph{un desayuno}
  \item \emph{el pan del desayuno}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What are the two pieces of \emph{desayuno}? (\emph{Des-}, undoing, and \emph{ayuno}, a fast.) And why did anatomists call one stretch of gut the jejunum? (They kept finding it empty.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la fruta]{la fruta — what a plant gives you back}

\label{lesson:ES-C367-fruta}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the wardrobe}, then \emph{breakfast}. (\emph{El armario}; \emph{el desayuno}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la manzana — the one you can already name.
  \item el árbol — where most of it grows.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{FRU-ta}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{r} is a single tap, and the \emph{fr} runs together without a vowel sneaking in between. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la fruta} — \textquotedblleft{}fruit.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{frūctus} meant the yield of something — what it produced, what you got out of it. It was built on the verb \textbf{fruī}, \textquotedblleft{}to enjoy, to make use of.\textquotedblright{} So a fruit is not first a sweet round thing. It is \textbf{the enjoyment a plant hands back} to whoever tended it.

That older sense survives in English wherever \emph{fruit} steps away from the greengrocer: the fruits of your labour, a fruitful meeting, fruitless effort.

Three relatives, and the road each one took matters:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{fruit} came through Old French, which is why the Latin \emph{-ct-} wore off it;
  \item \textbf{frugal} came through French too, from \emph{frūx}, a sister noun meaning produce or crops. A frugal life is one lived on what the ground actually yields;
  \item \textbf{fructose} was assembled in a laboratory in the nineteenth century out of the Latin stem and a chemist's ending. Nobody inherited it. It kept the \emph{-ct-} because it was built from the spelling, not passed down by mouth.
\end{itemize}

There is one more, and it does not look related at all. English \textbf{brook}, in \emph{she will brook no argument}, is the inherited Germanic cousin of the same ancient root. It once meant to use or enjoy a thing, and narrowed over centuries to putting up with it. Enjoy and endure, from one starting point.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now name the class as well as the item: \emph{la manzana es una fruta}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la fruta}
  \item \emph{una fruta}
  \item \emph{la manzana es una fruta}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Latin \emph{fruī} mean? (To enjoy, to make use of.) And what does a frugal person live on? (What the ground yields.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la naranja]{la naranja — the fruit that lent English a colour}

\label{lesson:ES-C367-naranja}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{breakfast}, then \emph{fruit}. (\emph{El desayuno}; \emph{la fruta}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la fruta — the class this one belongs to.
  \item el color — because in Spanish, as in English, this word does both jobs.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{na-RAN-ja}, three beats with the weight on the second. The \emph{j} is the scraping sound at the back of the mouth, nothing like an English \emph{j}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la naranja} — \textquotedblleft{}the orange.\textquotedblright{}

This word walked to Spain, and you can follow its footprints backwards. Arabic \textbf{nāranj}. Persian \textbf{nārang}. Sanskrit \textbf{nāraṅga}, and probably a loan into Sanskrit before that, from further south in India. Spanish took the Arabic form with its first \emph{n} still on the front.

English got the same word and dropped that \emph{n}. Somewhere in Romance the phrase was reheard: \textbf{a norange} turned into \textbf{an orange}, and the consonant walked across to the article. That is a reconstruction rather than a recorded event, but English has done the identical thing to itself twice where the paperwork survives:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{an apron} was once \emph{a napron};
  \item \textbf{a newt} was once \emph{an ewte}, and took an \emph{n} it had no right to.
\end{itemize}

Portuguese has \textbf{laranja}, with an \emph{l} where Spanish has \emph{n}. Nobody has a convincing account of why, and the honest thing is to notice it rather than explain it.

Now the part people find hard to believe. The \textbf{colour} is named after the \textbf{fruit}. English has no record of the word as a colour until the sixteenth century, because before the fruit came north there was no ordinary word for that shade — writers reached for compounds of yellow and red. A carrot, a sunset and a traffic cone are all named after a piece of fruit.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now name a fruit and a colour with one word: \emph{la naranja}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la naranja}
  \item \emph{una naranja}
  \item \emph{la naranja es una fruta}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which language did \emph{naranja} reach Spanish from? (Arabic.) And which came first in English, the fruit or the colour? (The fruit — the colour was named after it.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la patata]{la patata — two American words in one}

\label{lesson:ES-C367-patata}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{fruit}, then \emph{the orange}. (\emph{La fruta}; \emph{la naranja}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la comida — what this ends up inside.
  \item la tierra — where it grows, out of sight.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pa-TA-ta}, three beats with the weight on the second. Both \emph{t} sounds are made with the tongue against the teeth, softer than an English \emph{t}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la patata} — \textquotedblleft{}the potato.\textquotedblright{}

Two plants, two American languages, one Spanish word — and a muddle nobody ever tidied up.

\textbf{Batata} is Taíno, an Arawakan language of the Caribbean islands, and it named the \textbf{sweet} potato. \textbf{Papa} is Quechua, from the Andes, and it named the tuber you would recognise as a potato. Spanish met both plants within a few decades of each other, and the standard reading of \emph{patata} is that the two names ran together.

The muddle is still on the map. Much of Latin America says \textbf{papa} and holds the two plants apart with separate words. Spain says \emph{patata} for the ordinary one. Both are Spanish; neither is a mistake, and you will be understood either way.

English took \emph{patata} and made \textbf{potato} of it — and for its first decades in English, a potato was the \textbf{sweet} one. The white potato borrowed the name afterwards, from the plant that had it first.

One warning worth carrying. Quechua \emph{papa}, the tuber, has nothing to do with \textbf{papá}, father. That one is a nursery word, the sound a small child makes early, and dozens of unrelated languages arrived at it on their own.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now name what grows underground: \emph{la patata}, and \emph{la papa} where they say it that way.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la patata}
  \item \emph{una patata}
  \item \emph{la patata está en la tierra}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two American languages are read into \emph{patata}? (Taíno and Quechua.) And which plant did English call a potato first? (The sweet potato.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el azúcar]{el azúcar — the article that came along with the word}

\label{lesson:ES-C367-azucar}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the orange}, then \emph{the potato}. (\emph{La naranja}; \emph{la patata}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la miel — what sweetened food before this arrived.
  \item el café — the usual reason to reach for it.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{a-ZÚ-car}, three beats with the weight on the second, which is why the accent is written: a word ending in \emph{-r} would otherwise carry its weight at the end. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el azúcar} — \textquotedblleft{}sugar.\textquotedblright{}

Start with the front of the word, because the front of the word is not part of the word.

Arabic marks a definite noun with \textbf{al-}, and before certain letters that \emph{l} assimilates to whatever follows. Before \emph{s} it becomes \textbf{as-}. Arabic for the sugar is \textbf{as-sukkar}, and Spanish borrowed the whole phrase without noticing the seam. So \emph{el azúcar} carries two definite articles stacked on one noun, a Spanish one and an Arabic one.

Behind the Arabic stands a Persian form, and behind that Sanskrit \textbf{śarkarā}, which meant \textbf{grit, gravel}. Somebody looked at a heap of dried sugar, broken up for carrying, and reached for the word for coarse sand.

English \textbf{sugar} is the same eastern word, but it arrived through French rather than through Spanish — which is why English kept the sugar and left the article behind.

And English holds that Sanskrit word a second time, from the other end of the sea route: \textbf{jaggery}, the dark palm sugar, came through the languages of south India and then Portuguese. Two borrowings of one word, centuries apart, arriving from opposite directions.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now say how you take it: \emph{con azúcar}, \emph{sin azúcar}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el azúcar}
  \item \emph{con azúcar}
  \item \emph{un café con azúcar}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the \emph{a-} at the front of \emph{azúcar}? (The Arabic article \emph{al-}, assimilated to \emph{as-}.) And what did Sanskrit \emph{śarkarā} mean? (Grit, gravel.)
\end{tcolorbox}
